To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) trends in the carbon system emerge faster than trends in the physical climate system, (2) the ToE is mainly determined by the natural variability and (3) the ToE can be reduced if seasonal observations are used to represent the annual cycle.

(a) the time of emergence of trends is a crucial measure for detecting anthropogenic climate change and (b) it depends on both the strength of a trend signal and the magnitude of natural variability, which is in turn affected by the seasonal signal.

(1) the time of emergence is shorter in ocean biogea-chemical variables than in the physical climate system, and that (2) natural variability is the dominant factor for determining the time of emergence, while the strength of the signal is of secondary importance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how long we need to wait before we can detect trends in ocean biogechemistry.
the detection of climate and carbon cycle change
the question of whether the trends are detectable in the presence of the natural variability, i.e. how long it takes until the signal is detectable.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ToE of a trend signal depends strongly on the variable and the area considered.
the ToE for a given signal depends strongly on the spatial and temporal resolution of the observations and the background noise.
ToE of trends in ocean variables depends on the specific variable and location.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ToE is an important concept for climate change detection, but it is strongly influenced by the natural variability in the system.
the ToE of the ocean carbon cycle variables are much shorter than the time required to detect the corresponding physical climate trends.
, for the detection of trends in oceanic biogeochemical properties, the ToE is much shorter than for the physical climate system, yet it is still of decadal order.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ToE of ocean biogeochemically important variables is significantly shorter than the ToE of physical variables, and that it is of the same order as the duration of current observations.
the ToE is not only determined by the strength of the signal and the noise but also by the seasonality of the noise.

, in the case of the ocean biogeo-chemistry, the ToE is shorter and the detectability of the trend is better than for SST, which has important implications for the design of observational programs and for the interpretation of observations.
